cultural.vision_reason: The image shows a wide hand-woven strip-cloth gown (tobe/boubou) with cotton embroidery panels, a classic West African garment form worn across the Sahel including by Wolof men; the specific embroidery pattern name is Hausa-associated but such robes circulate and are worn by many regional groups, so it fits the claimed ethnicity.

physical.title: gown; tobe
physical.summary: Gown (tobe, boubou, riga): oblong shaped body with wide flared sleeves. Composed of 141 narrow strips about 2 ¼ inches wide, hand-woven with pale yellow-green hand-spun cotton, and hand-sewn together along the selvedges. Some strips have been folded double to produce the flare on the main tunic. A large pocket (which is now sewn up) has been sewn onto the front, and both front and back have been extensively embroidered in three shades of green cotton. The embroidery is in chain and buttonhole eyelet stitch, and in the ‘eight knives’ (aska takwas) pattern; there is a large spiral at the front and another on the back. The knives themselves are embroidered on top of extra pieces of cloth that have been cut to shape. The tunic is hemmed around the neck and sleeves, and has not been lined.
